C-H Activation Hot Paper
Asymmetric Ruthenium-Catalyzed C � H Activation by a Versatile
Chiral-Amide-Directing Strategy
Wenkun Chen, Jijun Jiang, and Jun Wang*
Abstract: A versatile and readily available chiral amide
directing group has been developed for the ruthenium-
(II)-catalyzed asymmetric C � H activation. Asymmetric
C � H activation of the related chiral benzamides with
various olefins, aldehydes and propargylic alcohols has
been accomplished with high stereoselectivities, afford-
ing a series of chiral products including 3,4-dihydroiso-
coumarins (up to 96 % ee), isocoumarins (up to 92 % ee),
phthalides (up to 99 % ee), chiral bicyclo[2.2.1]heptanes
(> 20 : 1 dr), 4-alkylidene-3,4-dihydroisocoumarins (up to
97 % ee) and allenes (> 20 : 1 dr). Importantly, our
methodologies enabled concise syntheses of many bio-
logically active compounds and natural products (e.g.,
Montroumarin, Cyclosporone E, Cyclosporone Q, Con-
centricolide, Chuangxinol, and Eleutherol).
Introduction
Transition-metal-catalyzed, directing-group assisted asym-
metric C � H activation enables enantioselective construc-
tions of diverse valuable chiral compounds from cheap
fundamental chemical feedstocks.
[1]
It proceeds in a highly
atom- and step-economic fashion, featuring a sequential
process of cleavage of an inert C � H bond and then
functionalization. It is well known that palladium, rhodium,
and ruthenium are currently three most widely used
transition metals to catalyze C � H activation. However, in
terms of asymmetric C � H activation, although
palladium-
[1h,2]
and rhodium-catalysis
[1a,h,3]
have achieved lots
of progress, the ruthenium-catalysis
[4]
remains in its infancy.
Given the excellent catalytic performance of [RuCl
2
(p-
cymene)]
2
in C � H activation,
[5]
which was first revealed by
Oi and Inoue,
[6]
three strategies are reasonably deduced to
make the corresponding reactions asymmetric.
[4]
The first
one is the usage of a chiral directing group. In 2019, Cui
[7a]
and Wang
[7b]
independently reported an intramolecular
hydroarylation of alkenes assisted by a chiral transient
directing group. Very recently, Gandon and Sahoo reported
an asymmetric two-fold C � H activation/annulation process
assisted by a chiral sulfoximine directing group.
[8]
The
second is the employment of a chiral carboxylic acid, which
was elegantly demonstrated by Ackermann,
[9]
Shi,
[10]
Yoshi-
no and Matsunaga
[11]
from 2021. The third is to replace p-
cymene in [RuCl
2
(p-cymene)]
2
with a chiral benzene ligand,
which was first revealed by Wang in 2022.
[12]
Besides, an
asymmetric relay catalysis involving ruthenium-catalyzed
C � H activation followed by a chiral amine-promoted
asymmetric intramolecular Michael addition was also re-
ported by Dethe.
[13]
It is noteworthy that, despite its high potential for
achieving ruthenium-catalyzed asymmetric C � H activation,
the strategy of utilizing chiral directing group(DG*) remains
largely overlooked by the community.
[14]
And the chiral
directing group with wide applications is still missing. Here-
in, a broadly useful chiral amide directing group derived
from commercially available and cheap (R)-α,α-diphenylpro-
linol is presented (Scheme 1). Assisted by it, asymmetric
C � H activation of chiral benzamide with olefins, aldehydes,
ketones, and propargylic alcohols have been accomplished
with high diastereoselectivities, affording various chiral
products with diverse chiral elements including 3,4-dihydroi-
socoumarins (center chirality, up to 96 % ee), 4-alkylidene-
3,4-dihydroisocoumarins (center chirality, up to 97 % ee),
isocoumarins (C � N axial chirality, up to 92 % ee), phthalides
(center chirality, up to 99 % ee), chiral bicyclo[2.2.1]heptanes
(center chirality, > 20 : 1 dr) and allenes (axial chirality,
> 20 : 1 dr). It is worth noting that our methodologies can
enable concise syntheses of several biologically active
compounds and natural products (e.g., Montroumarin,
Cyclosporone E, Cyclosporone Q, Concentricolide, Chuang-
xinol, and Eleutherol).
Results and Discussion
Reaction with Alkenes
Chiral 3,4-dihydroisocoumarins widely exist in bioactive
compounds and natural products.
[15]
Although several cata-
lytic asymmetric syntheses of 3,4-dihydroisocoumarins have
been reported,
[16]
the employed substrates or chiral catalysts
are normally not easily available. In recent years, transition-
metal catalyzed C � H activation turns out to be a straightfor-
ward strategy to synthesize various 3,4-dihydroisocoumarins
by reaction of benzoic acids
[17]
or amides
[18]
with epoxides or
alkenes, which are all facilely available. However, the
related asymmetric catalysis is challenging and has not been
achieved yet. Herein, we present the first example of

Under the optimized reaction conditions indicated in
Scheme 2 (for reaction condition optimizations, see Support-
ing Information), various chiral amides 1 derived from (R)-
α,α-diphenylprolinol were subjected to react with substituted
styrenes, giving chiral 3-substituted 3,4-dihydroisocoumarins
in moderate to good yields with high ee values. Benzamides
bearing electron-withdrawing or electron-donating substitu-
ents were all tolerable (3 a–h). The reaction of the chiral
amide 1 b with styrene could be conducted on gram scale
(3.0 mmol), affording 3 b in 58 % yield with 92 % ee. The
product 3 i was obtained solely when 3-methyl substituted
benzamide was tested. 2-Methyl substituted benzamide 1 j
was unreactive. 2-Naphthoic acid derived and two multi-
substituted benzamides were also suitable substrates for this
transformation (3 k–m). Cyclohexene-1-carboxamide af-
forded product in reasonable yield with 76 % ee (3 n). The
indole derived product 3 o was also obtained in 44 % yield
with 90 % ee. With 4-MeO substituted benzamide as model
substrate, various substituted styrenes were then evaluated.
All gave reasonable yields and high ee values (3 p–v).
Additionally, by this protocol, Adapalene, a retinoid drug
for the treatment of acne, could be smoothly converted to
the corresponding 3,4-dihydroisocoumarin 3 w in 48 % yield
with 90 % ee. However, the reaction of 3 a with aliphatic
alkenes such as 1-hexene was unsuccessful.
When N-aryl maleimides were tested, interestingly,
isocoumarins 5 were generated instead of 3,4-dihydroisocou-
marins, possibly by a sequential oxyarylation-dehydrogen-
ation process (Scheme 3). And silver carbonate should play
as the oxidant. To our delight, when N-2-

axial chirality were successfully obtained in 42–61 % yield
with 80–92 % ee under slightly modified reaction conditions.
Furthermore, the chiral benzamide 1 a was also at-
tempted to react with norbornene 6.

hydroarylation product 7 a was obtained (92 % yield,

Reaction with Aldehydes
Phthalides are of great pharmaceutical
[23]
and synthetic
importance.
[24]
Many natural products are also phthalides.
[23]
In the past decades, great efforts have been devoted to their
synthesis,
[24–25]
including their asymmetric synthesis.
[24,25b]
It is
worth noting that transition-metal-catalyzed direct addition
of aryl C � H to aldehyde/ketones followed by lactonization
emerged as a highly efficient strategy for the construction of
various phthalides.
[26]
Attractively, reactants are simple and
readily available. However, the asymmetric variants remain
rare. In 2015, Cramer and co-workers
[27]
reported a chiral
rhodium(III)-catalyzed asymmetric intramolecular
Grignard-type addition of inert C � H bond to aldehydes
followed by annulation to give chiral phthalides (3 exam-
ples) in moderate enantioselectivities. In 2019, we
[28]
re-
ported a highly enantioselective synthesis of chiral phtha-
lides by a chiral transient directing group assisted,
rhodium(III) catalyzed Grignard-type addition of arene
C � H bond of one aldehyde to the carbonyl group of another
followed by annulation. In 2020, we
[29]
developed an
alternative synthesis of chiral 3-aryl substituted phthalides
by chiral rhodium(III)-catalyzed Grignard-type addition of
inert arene C � H bond of chiral benzamide to aldehyde
followed by lactonization. Despite these achievements, two
issues remain unresolved. First, previously reported methods
turned out to be ineffective to aliphatic aldehydes to give
chiral 3-alkyl substituted phthalides, which ubiquitously exist
in natural products and bioactive compounds. Second, the
previously reported methods are not economical enough for
practical uses considering (1) precious rhodium was used as
catalyst, (2) the chiral amines to form chiral directing groups
as well as the chiral cyclopentadienyl ligands are not facilely
available.
Herein, we present a highly diastereoselective
ruthenium(II)-catalyzed asymmetric C � H activation of chi-
ral (R)-α,α-diphenylprolinol-derived benzamides with alde-
hydes to afford various chiral phthalides. As shown in
Scheme 7, with chiral benzamide as the model substrate,
aromatic aldehydes bearing a wealth of functional groups in
the para-, ortho-, or meta-position were tested under the
optimized reaction conditions, furnishing phthalides in
moderate to good yields with high ee values (19 a–h). Then
various benzamides were allowed to react with 4-nitro-
benzaldehyde, giving the corresponding phthalides (19 i–o,
19 q–r) in good yields with high ee values. But the ortho-
methyl benzamide was unreactive probably due to the steric
hindrance. Interestingly, ethyl 3,3,3-trifluoropyruvate could
also be successfully converted to the desirable phthalide
(19 s). Notably, aliphatic aldehydes could also be applied,

phthalide natural products (Scheme 9).
To check the practicability of this methodology, we
attempted to perform the reaction of 1 a and 18 b on a large
scale of 2.5 mmol (Scheme 8a). Delightedly, the product 19 b
was obtained in 67 % yield with 99 % ee. It is worth noting
that the chiral oxazolidine byproduct 20 (cis:trans = 10 : 1)
was obtained, from which α,α-diphenylprolinol could be
facilely recovered through two steps in the form of Boc-
protected α,α-diphenylprolinol 21 without loss of any
enantiomeric purity (> 99 % ee) (Scheme 8b). This finding
also revealed why excessive aldehydes were required for this
catalytic reaction.
As shown in Scheme 9, our methodology has been
proved to be a highly efficient tool to construct various
enantiomerically enriched chiral phthalide natural products
and bioactive compounds. First, the Vermistatin
[30]
analogue
19 t was obtained in 40 % yield with 90 % ee by the reaction
of the chiral amide 1 k and the aldehyde 18 i (Scheme 9a).
Secondly, with the chiral amide 1 u as the substrate,
divergent synthesis of four phthalides 19 u–aa were accom-
plished in a single step from the corresponding aliphatic
aldehydes 18 j–m (Scheme 9b). Full demethylation by BBr
3
gave the natural product Cytosporone E (19 x),
[31]
Cytospor-
one Q (19 y),
[32]
19 z with in vitro growth inhibitory
activity,
[33]
and 19 ab in good yields without loss of enantio-
meric excesses. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first
asymmetric total synthesis of Cytosporone Q (19 y). The
phthalide 19 ab could be converted into the anti-HIV active
compound 19 ac.
[34]
Similarly, reaction of the chiral amide 1 q
with the aldehyde 18 n led to a straightforward synthesis of
the anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective molecule 19 ad
(Scheme 9c).
[35]
Reaction of the chiral amide 1 v with the
aldehyde 18 n gave a mixture of regioisomers 19 ae and
19 ae’ (5 : 1, 38 % overall yield). Although it is difficult to
separate them by column chromatography, pure (R)-
Chuangxinol (19 ae)
[36]
could be obtained with > 99 % ee by
a single recrystallization (75 % yield, Scheme 9d). Addition-
ally, (S)-Concentricolide (19 af) was successfully synthesized
from the chiral amide 1 w and propionaldehyde (18 o) in
45 % yield with 92 % ee (Scheme 9e), which is much shorter
than the reported synthetic routes.
[37]
Moreover, with the
chiral amide 1 x prepared from 3-methoxybenzaldehyde via
4 steps as the substrate, Eleutherol (19 ag)
[38]
could be
facilely synthesized in 35 % yield with 90 % ee. Notably,
although racemic Eleutherol has been previously synthe-
sized via 5—10 steps,
[39]
this work represents the first
asymmetric synthesis of Eleutherol. It should be mentioned
that Eleutherol is a key intermediate to synthesize Eleutho-
side A (19 ah, Scheme 9f).
[39a]
To shed some light on the reaction mechanism, some
control experiments were conducted. First, it was found
chiral bisarene ruthenium complexes Ru-A and Ru-B were
stereoselectively formed in high yields when the chiral
amide 1 a and 1 d were respectively treated with [Ru(p-
cymene)Cl
2
]
2
and AgPF
6
(Scheme 10a). Under standard
catalytic reaction conditions, p-cymeneRu
II
also reacted with
the chiral amide 1 a to form Ru-A quantitatively as
determined by
1
H NMR (Scheme 10b). If the aldehyde 18 b
was introduced and the reaction was allowed to continue to
run for another 36 h, the product 19 b was obtained in 55 %
yield with 99 % ee (Scheme 10c). In addition, when [Ru(p-
cymene)Cl
2
]
2
used in standard reaction conditions was
replaced with Ru-A, the reaction of 1 a with 18 b could still
proceed smoothly to give the product 19 b in 51 % yield with
99 % ee (Scheme 10c). Therefore, Ru-A should be the
precatalyst. Next, to further identify the real catalytically
active species, cross-scrambling experiments were conducted
(Scheme 10d). It was observed that the combined use of the
chiral amide 1 d with excessive Ru-A (50 mol %) only led to
the product 19 l (67 % yield, 92 % ee), while the combined
use of the chiral amide 1 a and excessive Ru-B (50 mol %)
only provided the product 19 b (51 % yield, 99 % ee). It
implied that the catalytically active ruthenium species was
generated from Ru-A or Ru-B by the dissociation of p-
cymene rather than the chiral amide. Finally, chiral-match-
ing studies were carried out, considering both the amide
substrate and the ruthenium catalyst were chiral in this
reaction (Scheme 10e). By taking the reaction of the amide
1 a and the aldehyde 18 b as the benchmark reaction, in the
presence of the precatalyst Ru-B, it was found that the (R)-
amide substrate led to the product with 99 % ee, whereas the
(S)-amide substrate led to the product with � 99 % ee (with
the opposite absolute configuration). The two reactions are
in similar yields (52 % and 61 %). When the racemic amide
was used, the racemic product was obtained in 55 % yield.
Accordingly, the stereoselectivity of this reaction should be
exclusively controlled by the chiral amide.
Based on the above results and previous studies,
[27–29]
a
plausible reaction mechanism is proposed (Scheme 11).
First, in the presence of AgPF
6
, the chiral amide 1 a reacts
with [Ru(p-cymene)Cl
2
]
2
to form the bisarene ruthenium
complex Ru-A. Upon the dissociation of p-cymene, the
catalytically active species Ru-A’ was generated. By the
assistance of acetate, the chiral amide substrate 1 a reacts
with Ru-A’ to form the intermediate I via the CMD
mechanism. Addition of C � Ru bond to the aldehyde 18
affords the intermediate II, which further cyclizes upon the
amide to give the ruthenium alkoxide intermediate III.

and forms the Zn alkoxide IV, which collapses upon

Reaction with Propargylic Alcohols
Inspired by the work by Li
[40]
and Gooßen
[41]
on the synthesis
of 4-benzylidene-3,4-dihydroisocoumarin from amide or
benzoic acid with propargylic alcohols by C � H activation,
we also attempted the reaction of the chiral amide 1 a with
2.0 equivalent of the racemic secondary propargylic alcohol
22 a (Scheme 12). It was found that the chiral amides
preferably reacted with one enantiomer of the propargylic
alcohol 22 a via a C � H hydroarylation/lactonization se-
quence, giving the 4-benzylidene-3,4-dihydroisocoumarins
23 a in 38 % yields with 97 % ee. Surprisingly, the alcohol
22 a was recovered in 33 % yield with 0 % ee, suggesting its
racemization occurred quickly under reaction conditions.
When 3.0 equivalent of the racemic secondary propargylic
alcohol 22 a was used, the product 23 a was obtained in an
improved yield of 62 % with 97 % ee. Chiral benzamides
with electron-donating or electron-withdrawing groups on
the para- and ortho-positions were tolerable (23 b–e). The
enantioselectivity of the reaction decreased along the
decrease of the steric bulk of the R substituent of
propargylic alcohols (23 f–g). Both the yield and ee value
decreased if R was phenyl (23 h).

C onclusion
In summary, we describe a versatile and readily available
chiral amide directing group for ruthenium-catalyzed asym-
metric C � H bond activation of amides with olefins,
aldehydes, and propargylic alcohols. A series of chiral
products including 3,4-dihydroisocoumarins, isocoumarins,
phthalides, chiral bicyclo[2.2.1]heptanes, 4-alkylidene-3,4-
dihydroisocoumarins, and allenes were prepared in good
yields with high stereoselectivities. Moreover, asymmetric
syntheses of many natural products and bioactive com-
pounds, such as Montroumarin, Cyclosporone E, Cyclo-
sporone Q, Concentricolide, Chuangxinol, and Eleutherol,
have been achieved very concisely by using this method-
ology as the key step.
